depending on the position of
\Lambda
.

This map physically corresponds to the screening of the local operators by the condensed symmetry charges in the low energy subspace, such a screening defines a renormalization step on the space of local operators. The insertion of observables to the tensor network representation of the partition function is the so-called impurity tensor in the literature
[
71
,
72
]
. Along the tensor network renormalization process, the impurity tensor is constantly acted by tensors in the environment, and finally most details are screened out and only left with some finite data. Here, for a gapped system, the screening map is an idempotent
\mathrm{scr}^{2}=\mathrm{scr}
, whose image
\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{scr})=:\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
is called the algebra of fixed-point operators in the bulk.
Using the property of the Q-system, for
H
-type ground state
\omega
, we have

\omega=\omega\circ\mathrm{scr}.

Thus the
H
-type ground state space is isomorphic to the space of states on
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
.

An explicit form of space of states on
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
can be given.
In Proposition
G.1
, we show

\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)\simeq\hom_{\mathrm{fgt}A|\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}A,\mathrm{fgt}A)\simeq Z(\mathrm{fgt}A)
.
We thus decompose the algebra as
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)\simeq\oplus_{\alpha}\mathbb{C}p_{\alpha}
, with
\{p_{\alpha}\}
being the set of orthogonal projectors. Suppose for any
O\in\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}
,
\mathrm{scr}(O)=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}
, then
\omega(O)
is fully determined by
\{\omega\left(p_{\alpha,\{0\}}\right)\}_{\alpha}
, i.e.
\omega(O)=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}\,\omega(p_{\alpha,\{0\}})
. On the other hand, the
H
-type ground state of the Q-system model
(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A,1-m^{\dagger}m)
form a simplex, the extreme points of which are
\omega_{\alpha}
, satisfying
\omega_{\alpha}(m_{i,i+1}^{\dagger}m_{i,i+1})=1
for any
i
, and
\omega_{\alpha}\left(p_{\beta,\{0\}}\right)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}
. This establishes the bijection between the space of
H
-type ground states and the space of states on
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
(See Appendix
G.1
for detailed proofs).

Proposition V.3
.

Let
{\mathsf{H}}
be a finite dimensional Hopf C
⋆
-algebra and
(A,m,\iota)
a Q-system in
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}({\mathsf{H}})
. The Q-system model
(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A,1-m^{\dagger}m)
has the unique ground state if and only if
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)\simeq\mathbb{C}
, or equivalently,
\mathrm{fgt}A
is a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
.

Proof.

Suppose the Q-system model has a unique ground state, then the
O
-type ground state should just be the
H
-type ground state. By proposition
G.2
, the space of
H
-type ground states is isomorphic to the state space of
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
. Thus
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)\simeq\mathbb{C}
.

Conversely, suppose
\mathrm{fgt}A
is a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
, by propositions
G.2
and
V.2
, its
H
-type ground state is unique and is also the unique
O
-type ground state.
∎

We obtain:

The Q-system model
(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A,1-m^{\dagger}m)
is in a symmetric phase only if
\mathrm{fgt}A
is a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
.

In our construction in Section
II.2
, we choose
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}=\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
,
\omega=-1\in H^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2},U(1))
and define the Q-systems as:

•

A_{0}=\mathbb{C}e
,

•

A_{1}=\mathbb{C}^{\omega}\langle r^{2},s\rangle
,

•

A_{2}=\mathbb{C}^{\omega}\langle r^{2},sr\rangle
.

These Q-systems are all simple in
\mathsf{Hilb}
. In fact, they represent only three Q-systems (up to Morita equivalence) in
\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
and become simple Q-systems in
\mathsf{Hilb}
, i.e. when the
D_{8}
-grading structure is forgotten.

V.2
Examples of matrix algebras in
\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
and
\mathsf{Hilb}_{S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}}

Q-systems in
\mathsf{Hilb}_{G}
are classified into Morita classes, each determined by a pair
(H,\psi)
, where
H\subset G
is a subgroup up to conjugation and
\psi\in H^{2}(H,U(1))
is a 2-cocycle up to conjugation
\psi(g,h)\sim\psi(kgk^{-1},khk^{-1})

[
59
]
, and can be represented by the twisted group algebra
\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[H]
.

The subgroups of
D_{8}
up to conjugation are:

\displaystyle\langle e\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_{1},\ \langle r^{2}\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{(0)},\ \langle s\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{(1)},\ \langle sr\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{(2)},

\displaystyle\langle r^{2},sr\rangle=(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(2)},\ \langle r^{2},s\rangle=(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(1)},

\displaystyle\langle r\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_{4},\ D_{8}\,.

Among these, two subgroups isomorphic to
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
admit non-trivial cocycles, thus can be matrix algebras in
\mathsf{Hilb}
. Additionally,
D_{8}
itself admits non-trivial cocycles since
H^{2}(D_{8},U(1))\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. However, the twisted group algebra
\mathrm{fgt}\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[D_{8}]
cannot be simple in
\mathsf{Hilb}
, even in the presence of a non-trivial cocycle, simply because there is no matrix algebra with dimension
8
. By central extension of
D_{8}
to
D_{16}
, we know that
\mathrm{fgt}\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[D_{8}]=\mathbb{M}_{2}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}

[
73
]
.
Thus, the algebras
A_{0}
,
A_{1}
, and
A_{2}
are the only ones that satisfy the condition of the symmetric phase. These
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
-symmetric phases can, in fact, be understood as gauging the
D_{8}
symmetry of different SSB phases with
D_{8}
symmetry: the
D_{8}
fully SSB phase, the partial SSB partial SPT phase with a residual
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(1)}
symmetry, and the partial SSB partial SPT phase with a residual
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(2)}
symmetry.

More generally, we consider the twisted group algebra
\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p}]
, where
\psi\in H^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p},U(1))\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}
. We choose the “bi-character gauge” for the cocycles:

\psi(g,h)=\lambda^{g_{2}h_{1}},

where
\lambda
is a
p
-th root of unity. For
\lambda\neq 1
and
p
being prime, it is straightforward to verify that

Z(\mathrm{fgt}\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p}])\simeq\mathbb{C}.

Thus,
\mathrm{fgt}\mathbb{C}^{\psi}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p}]
is a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
whenever
p
is prime and
\psi
is non-trivial.

Next we consider
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3})
-symmetric phases, which has been discussed in the talk
[
74
]
. Up to conjugation, the possible subgroups are:

\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}_{1},\quad\mathbb{Z}_{2},\quad\mathbb{Z}_{3}^{(1)},\quad\mathbb{Z}_{3}^{(2)},\quad\mathbb{Z}_{3}^{(\mathrm{diag})},

\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3},\quad S_{3},\quad\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3},\quad S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}\,.

Since all cohomology groups of these subgroups are trivial except for
\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}
, the only possibility for symmetric phases arises when we consider the following twisted group algebras:

A_{0}:=\mathbb{C}_{e},\quad A_{\pm}:=\mathbb{C}^{\psi_{\pm}}[\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}],

where

\psi_{\pm}(g,h)=e^{\pm\frac{2\pi i}{3}g_{2}h_{1}}.

While we notice that two non-trivial 2-cocycles are identified as they are related by conjugating the non-trivial
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
element
s
. The 2-cocycle
\psi_{-}
is related to
\psi_{+}
via conjugation

\psi_{-}(g,h)=\psi_{+}(sgs^{-1},shs^{-1}).

Thus

\mathbb{C}^{\psi_{+}}[\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}]\simeq_{\mathrm{Mor}}\mathbb{C}^{\psi_{-}}[\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}].

There are two symmetric phases corresponding to:

A_{0},\quad A_{+/-},

where
A_{0}
describes the trivial SPT phase and
A_{+/-}
for the non-trivial SPT.

V.3
Edge mode

Edge modes are associated with the “ground state subspace” of a half-infinite chain. In this section, we focus on the
H
-type ground state subspace of the Q-system model on a half-infinite chain. Specifically, we consider the right half-infinite chain, noting that the analysis for the left half-infinite chain is analogous.

Similar to the discussion in the previous section, we consider the map of the
H
-type ground state on any local operator for any
\Lambda\in\mathfrak{S}^{f}_{\mathbb{N}}
. Take a finite subregion
\Xi=\{0,1,\cdots,\max(\Lambda)+1\}
and denote
m_{\Xi}:M\underset{}{\otimes}A^{\otimes(|\Xi|-1)}\rightarrow M
as the multiplication from
M\underset{}{\otimes}A^{\otimes(|\Xi|-1)}
to
M
, the module associativity implies the notation
m_{\Xi}
is independent of the multiplication order and thus well-defined. Let
O\in\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda}
, by subsequently apply the Equation (
11
), we have

\omega(O)=\omega(m_{\Xi}^{\dagger}\,m_{\Xi}\,O\,m_{\Xi}^{\dagger}\,m_{\Xi}).

We thus define the screening map

\displaystyle\mathrm{scr}:\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathfrak{A}_{\{0\}},

\displaystyle O

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathrm{scr}(O):=m_{\Xi}Om_{\Xi}^{\dagger},

The screening map physically corresponds to the screening of the boundary local operators by the condensed symmetry charges in the low energy subspace in the bulk, such a screening defines a renormalization step on the space of boundary local operators. The
\mathrm{scr}
is an idempotent and its image
\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{scr})=:\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
is called the algebra of fixed-point operators on the edge.
By the property of the Q-system model, we also have

\omega=\omega\circ\mathrm{scr}.

Thus the
H
-type ground state space is isomorphic to the space of states on
\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
.

Proposition V.4
.

Let
(A,m,\iota)
be a Q-system in
\mathsf{Hilb}
and
(M,m_{M})
an isometric right
A
-module. Then
\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M):=\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{scr})\simeq\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
.

When
\mathrm{fgt}A\simeq W\underset{}{\otimes}W^{*}
is a matrix algebra, take
A
itself as the boundary condition, then the algebra of fixed-point operators on the edge is
\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}A)=\mathrm{End}(W)
. The Hilbert space
W
is the so-called edge mode. In other words, the edge mode is the effective ground state subspace of the half-infinity chain, which can be reconstructed from the representation of the algebra of boundary fixed-point operators:

The edge mode of
(\mathbb{N},{\mathsf{H}},A,1-m^{\dagger}m,M,1-m_{M}^{\dagger}m_{M})
is the minimal faithful module over the algebra of fixed-point operators on edge
\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
.

There is a natural bulk-to-edge map that sends the fixed-point operators in the bulk to that on the edge

\displaystyle C_{r}:\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M),

This is a special case of the general mathematical principle called the bulk-edge correspondence for topological phases proposed in
[
54
,
75
]
.

In Appendix
G.2
, the general edge mode
M
between
A
and
B
phases is also considered.

The stability of the ground-state subspace requires that a symmetric operator, when restricted to this subspace, be proportional to the identity operator.
Therefore, the edge mode of
(\mathbb{N},{\mathsf{H}},A,1-m^{\dagger}m,M,1-m_{M}^{\dagger}m_{M})
is stable against symmetric perturbations if and only if
\dim\left({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}\right)_{A}\left(M,M\right)=1
, i.e.
M
is simple in
\left({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}\right)_{A}
. And the edge mode
N
between
A
-phase and
B
-phase is stable against symmetric perturbations if and only if
N
is simple in
{}_{A}\left({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}\right)_{B}
.

VI
Categorical aspects

Here, we investigate how the monoidal equivalence in the symmetry category
{\cal C}
induces an algebra in the charge category
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
, realizing a phase with the same charge category. Then we specialize to the case of an SPT phase and propose that to characterize an SPT phase with non-invertible symmetry, we need to consider its charge category in addition to the fiber functor of the symmetry category.

Theorem VI.1
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a fusion category and
{\cal M}
be an indecomposable finite semisimple left
{\cal C}
-module category. Let the dual category be
{{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}}:=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})
. Suppose
\pi:{\cal C}\to{\cal C}
is a monoidal equivalence, then
\pi
induces an algebra
A_{\pi}
in
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
such that
{}_{A_{\pi}}({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})_{A_{\pi}}\cong{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
;

Proof.

{\cal M}
induces a 2-equivalence between the 2-category of left
{\cal C}
-module categories and the 2-category of right
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
-module categories, known as the categorical Morita equivalence. More explicitly, denote the 2-equivalence functor by
F_{\cal M}
, then on objects, given a
{\cal C}
-module
{\cal N}
,

F_{\cal M}({\cal N})=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal N})
is a right
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
-module where the module action is simply the composition of module functors. On 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms (i.e.
{\cal C}
-module functors and natural transformations), for any pair of
{\cal C}
-modules
{\cal P},{\cal Q}
, we have equivalence functors
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal P},{\cal Q})\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{rev}}}(F_{\cal M}({\cal P}),F_{\cal M}({\cal Q}))
, where
({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{rev}}
is the same category as
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
but with opposite tensor product. This can be expanded to

\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal P},{\cal Q})\\
\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})^{\mathrm{rev}}}(\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal P}),\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal Q}))

(12)

and the equivalence is again induced by the post-composition of module functors.

Now consider the monoidal equivalence
\pi:{\cal C}\to{\cal C}
, we define a new left
{\cal C}
-module
{}_{\pi}{\cal M}
the module action of which is twisted by
\pi
:
c\underset{{}_{\pi}{\cal M}}{\triangleright}m:=\pi(c)\underset{{\cal M}}{\triangleright}m
. Automatically, we have
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({}_{\pi}{\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})
, where module functors
(F,s_{-,-})
are mapped to
(F,s_{\pi(-),-})
and module natural transformations are mapped to themselves. Under the categorical Morita equivalence
F_{\cal M}
,
F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M})=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})
and consequently

\displaystyle{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({}_{\pi}{\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{rev}}}(F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M}),F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M})).

Therefore,
F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M})
is an invertible
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
-
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
-bimodule.

For any module functor
Y\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})
, making use of the following internal hom adjunction

\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})(X,[Y,Y])\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})(YX,Y),

we can construct an algebra
[Y,Y]
in
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
such that
{}_{[Y,Y]}({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})\cong F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M})
. Choose any algebra
A_{\pi}
Morita equivalent to
[Y,Y]
in
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
, we then have

{}_{A_{\pi}}({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})\cong F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M})
and
{}_{A_{\pi}}({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})_{A_{\pi}}\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{rev}}}(F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M}),F_{\cal M}(_{\pi}{\cal M}))\cong{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
.
∎

{\cal C}
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
{\cal C}_{{\cal M}}^{\vee}
{\cal M}
{}_{\pi}{\cal M}
\mathsf{Fun}_{{\cal C}}({\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})
Duality

Figure 3:
Illustration of the categorical relationship of SPT phases.
{\cal C}
represents the symmetry category,
{\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
represents the charge category, and
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{}_{\pi}{\cal M})
represents the category of projective charges. Left
{\cal C}
module
{\cal M}
describes the lattice construction. For tensor product Hilbert space,
{\cal M}=\mathsf{Hilb}
.

Next, we prove a parallel result when considering
\mathsf{Hilb}
as a
{\cal C}
-module.
Firstly, we have monoidal equivalence

\displaystyle\mathsf{Hilb}

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Fun}(\mathsf{Hilb},\mathsf{Hilb})

\displaystyle W

\displaystyle\mapsto W\otimes-

\displaystyle\beta

\displaystyle\mapsto\beta\otimes\mathrm{id}_{-},

which also means that any natural transformation
W\otimes-\Rightarrow W^{\prime}\otimes-
must be of the form
\beta\otimes\mathrm{id}_{-}
for some linear map
\beta:W\to W^{\prime}
.

A
{\cal C}
-module structure on
\mathsf{Hilb}
is the same as a monoidal functor
f:{\cal C}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
. To emphasize the role of the monoidal functor, we denote its corresponding
{\cal C}
-module by
\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}
. Then note that there is a natural functor that forgets the module functor structure.

\displaystyle\mathrm{fgt}:{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{f})

\displaystyle\to\mathsf{Fun}(\mathsf{Hilb},\mathsf{Hilb})\cong\mathsf{Hilb}.

Theorem VI.2
.

Consider two monoidal functors
f,h:{\cal C}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
. There exist an algebra
A
in
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}
such that

1.

{}_{A}({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee})_{A}\cong{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}^{\vee}
;

2.

\mathrm{fgt}(A)
is a matrix algebra, or equivalently
\dim Z(\mathrm{fgt}(A))=1
.

Proof.

Let the linear dual of
W
be
W^{*}
, and
W^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}-
is automatically a left and right adjoint to
W\otimes-
as linear functors
\mathsf{Hilb}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
. We want to show that such adjointness lifts to
{\cal C}
-module functors. Suppose

W\underset{}{\otimes}-
equipped with natural isomorphisms
\beta_{c}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{-}:W\otimes f(c)\otimes-\cong h(c)\otimes W\otimes-
is a
{\cal C}
-module functor in
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})
. Then it is straightforward to check that
W^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}-
equipped with natural isomorphisms
(\beta_{c^{*}})^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{-}:W^{*}\otimes h(c)\otimes-\cong f(c)\otimes W^{*}\otimes-
is a
{\cal C}
-module functor in
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{h},\mathsf{Hilb}_{f})
and is moreover left and right adjoint to
W\otimes-
. This fact further implies the adjunction

\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{f})(X,W^{*}\otimes W\otimes-)\cong\\
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})(W\otimes X(-),W\otimes-).

We then know that

\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})\cong{}_{W^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}W\underset{}{\otimes}-}({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}).

Clearly
\mathrm{fgt}(W^{*}\otimes W\otimes-)=W^{*}\otimes W\cong\mathrm{End}(W)
is a matrix algebra. Since Morita equivalence is preserved by the linear monoidal functor
\mathrm{fgt}
, we conclude that for any algebra
A
Morita equivalent to
W^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}W\underset{}{\otimes}-
in
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
,
\mathrm{fgt}{A}
is Morita equivalent to a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
, thus must also be a matrix algebra.
∎

Corollary VI.3
.

Given a fusion category symmetry
{\cal C}
equipped with a fiber functor
f:{\cal C}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
, and a monoidal equivalence
\pi:{\cal C}\to{\cal C}
. We can take an algebra
A_{\pi}
in
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
via
{}_{A_{\pi}}({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee})\cong\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{f\pi})
. Then we have the following

–

{}_{A_{\pi}}({\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee})_{A_{\pi}}\cong{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f\pi}}^{\vee}\cong{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
;

–

\mathrm{fgt}(A_{\pi})
is a matrix algebra, or equivalently
\dim Z(\mathrm{fgt}(A_{\pi}))=1
.

{\cal C}
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}^{\vee}
\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}
\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}
\mathsf{Fun}_{{\cal C}}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})
Duality

Figure 4:
Illustration of the categorical relationship of SPT phases. Here the pair
({\cal C},f)
defines a symmetry as well as the trivial phase, and
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
the charge category corresponding to this symmetry. The pair
({\cal C},h)
defines another symmetry, whose charge category is
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}^{\vee}
, which may or may not be the same as
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
.

We show the converse by starting from the charge category
{\cal D}:={\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee}
and the forgetful functor:

Theorem VI.4
.

Fix a fiber functor
f:{\cal D}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
. Any algebra
A\in{\cal D}
such that
fA
is a matrix algebra in
\mathsf{Hilb}
, corresponds to a fiber functor
{\cal D}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}\to\mathsf{Hilb}
.

Proof.

Let

\underline{f}:{}_{A}{\cal D}_{A}\rightarrow{}_{fA}\mathsf{Hilb}_{fA}

be the monoidal functor induced from
f
.
By the Lemma 4.2, Theorem 4.9, and Remark 4.10 of
[
31
]
,

Z(f)
{}_{A}{\cal D}_{A}
\underline{f}
{}_{fA}\mathsf{Hilb}_{fA}
\mathsf{Hilb}
f
{\cal D}
{}_{A}{\cal D}
\mathsf{Hilb}
Z({\cal D})

we have the canonical equivalence

Z(\underline{f})\cong Z(f).

Since
fA\in\mathsf{Hilb}
is a simple algebra, there is a monoidal equivalence
{}_{fA}\mathsf{Hilb}_{fA}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}
.
Thus we have another fiber functor

Z(f)\cong Z(\underline{f})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{fgt}}{}_{fA}\mathsf{Hilb}_{fA}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}.

∎

An on-site symmetry is necessarily described by the pair
({\cal C},f:{\cal C}\to\mathsf{Hilb})
, which determines the microscopic realization of the fusion category symmetry along with a trivial phase.
More specifically,
{\cal C}
is some abstract fusion category and
f
describes its local structure.
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
is the corresponding charge category. For an object
(V\otimes-,\,\beta)\in{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
,
V
is the underlying Hilbert space of the symmetry charge, and
\beta_{c}:V\underset{}{\otimes}f(c)\cong f(c)\underset{}{\otimes}V
is the local tensor of the
c
-MPO acting on the space
V
. In
[
45
]
, the defects between two such pairs
({\cal C},f)
and
({\cal C},h)
form the category
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fun}(\Sigma{\cal C},2\mathsf{Hilb})}(\Sigma f,\Sigma h)=\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})
. Fixing
({\cal C},f)
as the trivial phase,
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})
is the category of edge-modes of
({\cal C},h)
. For a module functor
(W\underset{}{\otimes}-,\gamma)\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{f},\mathsf{Hilb}_{h})
,
W
is the edge mode and
\gamma_{c}:W\underset{}{\otimes}f(c)\rightarrow h(c)\underset{}{\otimes}W
is the local tensor of the
c
-MPO acting on the projective charge
W
. The internal hom tensors two opposite projective charges hence gives an algebra
A=(W^{*}\underset{}{\otimes}W\otimes-,\lambda)
in the charge category
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
. And
\dim Z(\mathrm{fgt}(A))=1
describes a symmetric state with a unique ground state in the thermodynamic limit.
In particular, when
\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}
and
\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}
are equivalent as
{\cal C}
-modules, i.e.,
W
is taken to be
\mathbb{C}
, then there is no edge mode, suggesting that
f
and
h
realize the same SPT phase, the trivial phase. Its corresponding algebra
\mathrm{End}(W)
is the trivial algebra in the charge category
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}
. Thus we define

Definition VI.5
.

Two pairs
({\cal C},f)
and
({\cal C},h)
, or two fiber functors
f,h
from
{\cal C}
, are called phase-equivalent if the corresponding
{\cal C}
-modules
\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}
and
\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}
are equivalent.

Then there exists a one-to-one correspondence between

•

the Morita classes of algebras in
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}
whose image under
\mathrm{fgt}
is Morita trivial (i.e. matrix algebras) in
\mathsf{Hilb}
,

•

and the phase-equivalent classes of fiber functors from
{\cal C}
.

However, there are further subtleties on the macroscopic observables associated with the pairs
({\cal C},f)
and
({\cal C},h)
. Two factors need to be taken into consideration:

•

whether
f
and
h
are related by a monoidal equivalence
\pi:{\cal C}\to{\cal C}
, i.e.
h=f\pi
;

•

whether the charge category is preserved
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
.

There are three possible scenarios:

1.

h=f\pi
induces a monoidal equivalence
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
and
({\cal C},f)
and
({\cal C},f\pi)
are not necessarily phase-equivalent. All the
G
-SPT phases and three
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
SPTs belong to this case;

2.

{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}\not\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
, where
h
and
f
are not related by monoidal equivalences. By Theorem
VI.2
, there exists an algebra
A
in
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}
such that
{}_{A}({\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}})_{A}\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
. We can construct a Q-system model with such algebra
A
and the fusion of defects is described by
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
. In such a model, the Hamiltonian is
({\cal C},f)
symmetric with a unique ground state. However, the fusion rules of the defects differ from the trivial phase, meaning that the charge category is not preserved. We view such a model as in a
locally
spontaneous symmetry-breaking phase. Unlike invertible symmetries, where a symmetry is broken to a subgroup, here the symmetry
({\cal C},f)
is broken to
({\cal C},h)
: the fusion category remains the same with the fiber functor changed. We emphasize that a fiber functor corresponds to the microscopic realization of the symmetry, consistent with the fact that in the locally SSB phase, only the fusion of defects is changed, which are local physical observables.

3.

There might be a situation landing in the middle of 1 and 2. It is possible that when
f
and
h
are not related by monoidal equivalences, it happens to be
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}
. It remains unclear what physical observables detect such an exotic case.

In general, the charge category of a fusion category symmetry is not unique, as discussed in scenario 2.
{\cal C}=\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3})
symmetry in Wen’s talk
[
74
]
is one such example; the charge category
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
given by the forgetful functor
f
is
\mathsf{Hilb}_{S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}}
. Following Theorems
VI.2
and
VI.4
, take
A_{+}=\mathbb{C}^{\psi_{+}}[\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}]
, we obtain a different charge category
{}_{A_{+}}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{S_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}})_{A_{+}}\cong\mathrm{TY}_{\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}}^{\chi,\epsilon}
, where
\chi(g,h)=\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi\mathrm{i}}{3}\left(g_{1}h_{2}+g_{2}h_{1}\right)\right]},\;\epsilon=1

6
6

6

Part of the result originated from a discussion with Conghuan Luo.
. See Appendix
H
for a detailed calculation. Another known example of scenario 2 is the isocategorical groups
[
49
]
. It states that when
{\cal C}
is a group representation category, its corresponding charge categories might have different underlying group structures, meaning that
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}_{G}
,
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{h}}^{\vee}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}_{G^{\prime}}
for non-isomorphic groups
G,G^{\prime}
.

In this paper, we focus on the case of
{\cal C}=\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
, where three fiber functors are related by monoidal equivalence. The module action of
{\cal C}
on
\mathsf{Hilb}
is fixed by the forgetful functor
\mathrm{fgt}:\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})\to\mathsf{Hilb}
. The charge category is
\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
and is preserved. Indeed we can show that
{}_{A_{\pi}}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}})_{A_{\pi}}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
. In Section
II
, we give an explicit lattice realization of the monoidal equivalence
\pi
via
{}_{A_{\pi}}(\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}})_{A_{\pi}}\cong\mathsf{Hilb}_{D_{8}}
and show that three SPT phases of
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
symmetry are permuted under such a construction.

By the classification result of
\mathsf{Rep}(G)
-module categories, the module category concerned in our
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
example is also equivalent to the category of projective representations
\mathsf{Rep}^{\omega\dagger}((\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(1),(2)})\cong\mathsf{Hilb}
. Here,
\omega=-1\in H^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2},U(1))
denotes the non-trivial cocycle.
The left
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
-module structures on
\mathsf{Rep}^{\omega\dagger}((\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(1),(2)})
are defined by
-\otimes W^{(1),(2)}
, where
W^{(1),(2)}
is the irreducible projective representation of
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{(1),(2)}
, respectively.

VII
Conclusion and discussion

In this work, we develop a framework to classify and construct (1+1)d SPT phases with fusion category symmetries. We focus on the kinematic role of the fiber functor, meaning how it defines an on-site symmetry operator, the charge category, and the trivial phase. We emphasize that a trivial phase is an integral component of the microscopic realization of an anomaly-free fusion category symmetry. We provide an alternative characterization of an SPT phase using the Q-system in the charge category. As an example, we study the
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}(D_{8})
-SPTs and realize the
S_{3}
-automorphism between three fiber functors via a duality transformation. Our construction applies to spontaneous symmetry breaking phases of a fusion category symmetry as well.

Our construction provided a generic framework for understanding non-invertible symmetry in (1+1)d and in higher dimensions. In particular, there is still much to explore in topological phases enriched by fusion category symmetries. One natural generalization is anomaly-free fermionic fusion category symmetry (for example
[
77
,
78
,
79
]
). Symmetry charges of a fermionic fusion category symmetry form a fusion category
{\cal D}
together with a monoidal functor to the category of super vector spaces
[
80
,
81
]
:

\mathrm{fgt}:{\cal D}\rightarrow{\mathsf{sVec}}.

To characterize the fermonic SPTs in terms of Q-systems, a subtlety lies in the fact that fermion parity is a preserved symmetry thus the ground state degeneracy is observed by operators with even fermion parity
[
5
]
. Therefore, a fermionic SPT is described by a Q-system
A
in
{\cal D}
, such that
\mathrm{fgt}(A)\in\mathsf{sVec}
is simple.

We could also consider higher-dimensional generalizations
[
82
,
83
]
. In
[
31
]
, the charge category of a 2D system is a fusion 2-category
[
84
]

\mathfrak{D}
. However, it remains unclear how to categorically describe the underlying 2D bosonic spin system and to understand local symmetry charges of
\mathfrak{D}
. A 2D bosonic spin system should be described by
2\mathsf{Vec}
, and the local symmetry charge realization is given by the 2-fiber functor
\mathfrak{D}\rightarrow 2\mathsf{Vec}
. However, in tensor product Hilbert space lattice models, we only have
\mathsf{Vec}
, the looping of the
2\mathsf{Vec}
. Thus how to incorporate the higher structure in
2\mathsf{Vec}
in a lattice model remains unclear.

On the other hand, if we relax the anomaly-free fusion category to those that do not admit a fiber functor, the anomalous symmetry category plays an essential role in understanding gapless phases. For example, anyonic chain construction can carry anomalous fusion category symmetries and can be used to explore critical phases
[
85
,
23
,
86
,
87
]
.

\eta^{e}=\prod_{j:\,even}X_{j},\quad\eta^{o}=\prod_{j:\,odd}X_{j}

unique ground state of which is a product state. Upon fixing the symmetry operators onsite, the cluster state can be chosen to be the trivial phase. Without the stacking structure of non-invertible SPTs, this choice of trivial phase is not canonical. In the second model (see Eqn.16 of

.
In

\displaystyle Z_{1}X_{2}Z_{3}|g,h,k\rangle=(-1)^{n_{s}(h)+1}|sg,h,sk\rangle.

We further group 2 cells into a single one, such that the local Hilbert space is

\mathbb{C}\{r,sr\}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathbb{C}\{r,sr\}=\mathbb{C}\{e,s,r^{2},sr^{2}\}

e=sr\,sr,\quad s=r\,sr,\quad r^{2}=r\,r,\quad sr^{2}=sr\,r.

Thus the final unit cell is composed with 4 original sites, labeled by the capital letters

.
The Hamiltonian is equivalent to

H=-\sum_{I}\frac{1}{4}(1-Z_{4I-3}X_{4I-1}Z_{4I+1})(1-Z_{4I-1}X_{4I+1}Z_{4I+3})=-\sum_{I}\tilde{P}_{I,I+1}\,.

Notice that

where

\displaystyle P_{I,I+1}=\frac{1}{4}(1+Z_{4I-3}X_{4I-1}Z_{4I+1})(1+Z_{4I-1}X_{4I+1}Z_{4I+3}),

\displaystyle\bar{P}_{L/4-1,L/4}=\frac{1}{4}(1+Z_{L-7}X_{L-5}Z_{L-3})(1-Z_{L-5}X_{L-3}Z_{L-1}),

\displaystyle\bar{P}_{L/4,1}=\frac{1}{4}(1-Z_{L-3}X_{L-1}Z_{1})(1+Z_{L-1}X_{1}Z_{3}).

with exceptions on the boundary, which correspond to local symmetric defects. Since a phase is at the thermodynamic limit, the phase realized in

The component of

\displaystyle P_{e}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,e&s\,s&r^{2}\,r^{2}&sr^{2}\,sr^{2}\\
\hline\cr e\,e&1&1&-1&1\\

r^{2}\,r^{2}&-1&-1&1&-1\\
sr^{2}\,sr^{2}&1&1&-1&1\\
\end{array},\quad P_{s}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,s&s\,e&sr^{2}\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr^{2}\\
\hline\cr e\,s&1&1&-1&1\\
s\,e&1&1&-1&1\\
sr^{2}\,r^{2}&-1&-1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,sr^{2}&1&1&-1&1\end{array},

\displaystyle P_{r^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,e&s\,sr^{2}&sr^{2}\,s\\
\hline\cr e\,r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,e&1&1&1&-1\\
s\,sr^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
sr^{2}\,s&-1&-1&-1&1\end{array},\quad P_{sr^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr^{2}&sr^{2}e&s\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,s\\
\hline\cr e\,sr^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
sr^{2}\,e&1&1&1&-1\\
s\,r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,s&-1&-1&-1&1\end{array}

Define

\displaystyle m_{e}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,e&s\,s&r^{2}\,r^{2}&sr^{2}\,sr^{2}\\
\hline\cr e&1&1&-1&1\end{array},\quad m_{s}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,s&s\,e&sr^{2}\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr^{2}\\
\hline\cr s&1&1&-1&1\end{array},

\displaystyle m_{r^{2}}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,e&s\,sr^{2}&sr^{2}\,s\\
\hline\cr r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\end{array},\quad m_{sr^{2}}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr^{2}&sr^{2}\,e&s\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,s\\
\hline\cr sr^{2}&1&1&1&-1\end{array}.

Then

P=\frac{1}{4}m^{\dagger}m.

We can then extract the cocycle gauge by
m
:

\omega(r^{2},r^{2})=\omega(sr^{2},r^{2})=\omega(r^{2},s)=\omega(sr^{2},s)=-1,\quad\omega(\text{others})=1.

Thus the Hamiltonian of
[
35
]
, for either
L=0\mod{8}
or
L=4\mod{8}
, matches our model locally

H=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i}m_{i,i+1}^{\dagger}m_{i,i+1}\,.

And the MPO
A_{\sigma}
acts on ground state as
\mathrm{Tr}(A_{\sigma})|e\rangle=2|e\rangle
.

The third model is constructed similarly. After applying the CZ gate, the ground state is stabilized by the generator

-X_{2n-1}=1,\quad-Z_{2n-2}X_{2n}Z_{2n+2}=1\,.

Imposing the constraint
X_{2n-1}=-1
, the local Hilbert space on a two-site unit cell is
\mathbb{C}\{s,r\}
.
In
|s\rangle,|r\rangle
basis,

Z=|s\rangle\langle s|-|r\rangle\langle r|,\quad X=|s\rangle\langle r|+|r\rangle\langle s|\,.

We then group 2 cells to form the final unit cell and

\mathbb{C}\{s,r\}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathbb{C}\{s,r\}=\mathbb{C}\{e,sr,r^{2},sr^{3}\}

with

e=s\,s,\quad sr=s\,r,\quad r^{2}=r\,r,\quad sr^{3}=r\,s.

After reversing the sign, the local projector between two nearby sites to the unique ground state is

P_{I,I+1}=\frac{1}{4}\left(1+Z_{4I}X_{4I+2}Z_{4I+4}\right)\left(1+Z_{4I+2}X_{4I+4}Z_{4I+6}\right)\,,

with

\displaystyle P_{e}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,e&sr\,sr&r^{2}\,r^{2}&sr^{3}\,sr^{3}\\
\hline\cr e\,e&1&1&-1&1\\
sr\,sr&1&1&-1&1\\
r^{2}\,r^{2}&-1&-1&1&-1\\
sr^{3}\,sr^{3}&1&1&-1&1\\
\end{array},\quad P_{sr}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr&sr\,e&sr^{3}\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr^{3}\\
\hline\cr e\,sr&1&1&1&-1\\
sr\,e&1&1&1&-1\\
sr^{3}\,r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,sr^{3}&-1&-1&-1&1\end{array},

\displaystyle P_{r^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,e&sr^{3}\,sr&sr\,sr^{3}\\
\hline\cr e\,r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,e&1&1&1&-1\\
sr^{3}\,sr&1&1&1&-1\\
sr\,sr^{3}&-1&-1&-1&1\end{array},\quad P_{sr^{3}}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr^{3}&sr^{3}\,e&sr\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr\\
\hline\cr e\,sr^{3}&1&1&-1&1\\
sr^{3}\,e&1&1&-1&1\\
sr\,r^{2}&-1&-1&1&-1\\
r^{2}\,sr&1&1&-1&1\end{array}

Define

\displaystyle m_{e}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,e&s\,s&r^{2}\,r^{2}&sr^{2}\,sr^{2}\\
\hline\cr e&1&1&-1&1\end{array},\quad m_{sr}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr&sr\,e&sr^{3}\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr^{3}\\
\hline\cr s&1&1&1&-1\end{array},

\displaystyle m_{r^{2}}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,e&sr^{3}\,sr&sr\,sr^{3}\\
\hline\cr r^{2}&1&1&1&-1\end{array},\quad m_{sr^{3}}=\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}&e\,sr^{3}&sr^{3}\,e&sr\,r^{2}&r^{2}\,sr\\
\hline\cr sr^{3}&1&1&-1&1\end{array}.

Then

P=\frac{1}{4}m^{\dagger}m.

We can then extract the cocycle gauge by
m
:

\omega(r^{2},r^{2})=\omega(r^{2},sr^{3})=\omega(sr,sr^{3})=\omega(r^{2},sr)=-1,\quad\omega(\text{others})=1.

Appendix B
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}({\mathsf{H}}^{*}_{8})
-MPOs on irreducible charges

We first list the data for
{\mathsf{H}}_{8}
:

{\mathsf{H}}_{8}=\Big\langle x,y,x|x^{2}=y^{2}=z^{2}=\mathbf{1},\,xz=zx,\,yz=zy,\,xyz=yx\Big\rangle\,,

with basis

\Big\{\mathbf{1},\,x,\,y,\,z,\,xz,\,yz,\,xy,\,yx\Big\},

where
z
is the central element. Thus we identify two central orthogonal idempotents

p_{0}=\frac{1}{2}(1+z),\quad p_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(1-z).

The counits are
\epsilon(x)=\epsilon(y)=\epsilon(z)=1
and the comultiplications are given by

\displaystyle\Delta 1=1\underset{}{\otimes}1,\quad\Delta x=xp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}x+xp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}y,\quad\Delta y=yp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}x+yp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}y,\quad\Delta z=z\underset{}{\otimes}z,

\displaystyle\Delta(xz)=(\Delta x)(\Delta z)=xp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}xz-xp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}yz,\quad\Delta(yz)=(\Delta y)(\Delta z)=-yp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}xz+yp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}yz,

\displaystyle\Delta(xy)=(\Delta x)(\Delta y)=xyp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}xy+xyp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}yx,\quad\Delta(yx)=yxp_{1}\underset{}{\otimes}xy+yxp_{0}\underset{}{\otimes}yx.

The antipode
S
is defined as

\displaystyle S(x)=xp_{0}+yp_{1},\quad S(y)=xp_{1}+yp_{0},\quad S(z)=z,

\displaystyle S(xy)=yx,\quad S(xz)=\frac{1}{2}(x-y+xz+yz),\quad S(yz)=\frac{1}{2}(-x+y+yz+xz),\quad S(yx)=xy.

The MPO basis
\Gamma=\Big\{{\hat{\mathbf{1}}},\,{\hat{a}},\,{\hat{b}},\,{\hat{c}},\,{\hat{\sigma}}^{11},\,{\hat{\sigma}}^{12},\,{\hat{\sigma}}^{21},\,{\hat{\sigma}}^{22}\Big\}
is explicitly given by the basis transformation

\displaystyle{\hat{\mathbf{1}}}=\mathbf{1},\quad{\hat{a}}=\frac{1+\mathrm{i}}{2}(xy-\mathrm{i}yx),\quad{\hat{b}}=\frac{1+\mathrm{i}}{2}(-\mathrm{i}xy+yx),\quad{\hat{c}}=z,

\displaystyle{\hat{\sigma}}^{11}=xp_{0},\quad{\hat{\sigma}}^{12}=xp_{1}\quad{\hat{\sigma}}^{21}=yp_{1},\quad{\hat{\sigma}}^{22}=yp_{0}.

Here we use hat to denote objects in
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}({\mathsf{H}}_{8}^{*})
and those without hat to denote objects in
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}({\mathsf{H}}_{8})
.
As a sanity check, we can show that the above basis satisfies MPO basis properties in
III.3
, meaning

–

multiplication:
{\hat{a}}{\hat{a}}={\hat{\mathbf{1}}},\;{\hat{b}}={\hat{a}}{\hat{c}}={\hat{c}}{\hat{a}}
;

–

comultiplication:
\Delta{\hat{a}}={\hat{a}}\underset{}{\otimes}{\hat{a}},\;\Delta{\hat{c}}={\hat{c}}\underset{}{\otimes}{\hat{c}},\;\Delta{\hat{\sigma}}^{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{\gamma}{\hat{\sigma}}^{\alpha\gamma}\underset{}{\otimes}{\hat{\sigma}}^{\gamma\beta}
;

–

antipode:
S({\hat{a}})={\hat{a}},\;S({\hat{c}})={\hat{c}},\;S({\hat{\sigma}}^{\alpha\beta})={\hat{\sigma}}^{\beta\alpha}
.

Representation category of
{\mathsf{H}}_{8}
is isomorphic to the Tambara-Yamagami category
\mathrm{TY}_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}^{\chi(g,h)=(-1)^{g_{1}h_{1}+g_{2}h_{2}},\epsilon=1}
. The irreducible representations are listed in Table
3
.

We then calculate
\mathsf{Rep}^{\dagger}({\mathsf{H}}_{8}^{*})
-MPOs on irreducible
{\mathsf{H}}_{8}
-charges. Invertible MPOs are:

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}})^{11}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}})^{11}_{a}=(T_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}})^{11}_{b}=(T_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}})^{11}_{c}=1,\quad(T_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}})^{11}_{\sigma}=\mathbf{1},

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{a}})^{11}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{a}})^{11}_{c}=1,\quad(T_{\hat{a}})^{11}_{a}=(T_{\hat{a}})^{11}_{b}=-1,\quad(T_{\hat{a}})^{11}_{\sigma}=-Z,

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{b}})^{11}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{b}})^{11}_{c}=1,\quad(T_{\hat{b}})^{11}_{a}=(T_{\hat{b}})^{11}_{b}=-1,\quad(T_{\hat{b}})^{11}_{\sigma}=Z,

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{c}})^{11}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{c}})^{11}_{a}=(T_{\hat{c}})^{11}_{b}=(T_{\hat{c}})^{11}_{c}=1,\quad(T_{\hat{c}})^{11}_{\sigma}=-\mathbf{1}.

And components of the non-invertible MPO are:

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{11}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{11}_{b}=\mathbf{1},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{11}_{a}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{11}_{c}=-\mathbf{1},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{11}_{\sigma}=\mathbf{0},

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{12}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{12}_{a}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{12}_{b}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{12}_{c}=\mathbf{0},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{12}_{\sigma}=X,

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{21}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{21}_{a}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{21}_{b}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{21}_{c}=\mathbf{0},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{21}_{\sigma}=Y,

\displaystyle(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{22}_{\mathbf{1}}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{22}_{a}=\mathbf{1},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{22}_{b}=(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{22}_{c}=-\mathbf{1},\quad(T_{\hat{\sigma}})^{22}_{\sigma}=\mathbf{0}.

Appendix C
Some basics of category theory

Definition C.1

(Module Category)
.

Let
({\cal C},\underset{}{\otimes},\mathbf{1},\alpha,\lambda,\rho)
be a linear monoidal category, where
\mathbf{1}
is the tensor unit,
\alpha,\,\lambda,\,\rho
are natural isomorphisms called associator, left unitor and right unitor respectively. A left module category over
{\cal C}
is a linear category
{\cal M}
equipped with a linear monoidal functor
{\cal C}\rightarrow\mathsf{Fun}({\cal M},{\cal M})
, or equivalently, a bilinear functor
\rhd:{\cal C}\times{\cal M}\rightarrow{\cal M}
with

•

An associator: a natural transformation
m
:
(-\underset{}{\otimes}-)\rhd-\Rightarrow-\rhd(-\rhd-)

\forall\,X,\,Y,\,Z\in{\cal C}
,
M\in{\cal M}
such that the functor
M\mapsto\mathbf{1}\rhd M:{\cal M}\rightarrow{\cal M}
is an autoequivalence, and such that the pentagon diagram commutes

Definition C.2

(
{\cal C}
-module functor)
.

{\cal M}
and
{\cal N}
be two module categories over
{\cal C}
with associativity constraints
m
and
n

{\cal M}
to
{\cal N}

F:{\cal M}\rightarrow{\cal N}
and a natural isomorphism

Definition C.3

(Internal Hom)
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a monoidal category and
{\cal M}
be a
{\cal C}
-module category. Given
M,\,N\in{\cal M}
. If the functor
X\mapsto{\cal M}(X\rhd M,N):{\cal C}\rightarrow\mathsf{Vec}
is representable, i.e., there exists an object
[M,N]\in{\cal C}
and a natural isomorphism

{\cal M}(X\rhd M,N)\cong{{\cal C}}(X,[M,N])\,,

then
[M,N]
is called the internal Hom.

Definition C.4

(
\mathsf{Hilb}_{G}
)
.

Let
G
be a finite group. The category of finite-dimensional
G
-graded Hilbert spaces, denoted by
\mathsf{Hilb}_{G}
, is a unitary fusion category consists of the following data:

–

objects:
G
-graded Hilbert spaces
V\simeq\oplus_{g\in G}V_{g}
, and for all
u_{g}\in V_{g}
and
v_{h}\in V_{h}
,
\langle u_{g}|v_{h}\rangle=0
if
g\neq h
;

–

morphisms:
G
-grading preserving linear maps;

–

the tensor product: given
G
-graded Hilbert spaces
V=\oplus_{g\in G}V_{g}
and
W=\oplus_{g\in G}W_{g}
, the
g
-graded subspace of
V\underset{}{\otimes}W
is
(V\underset{}{\otimes}W)_{g}=\oplus_{h\in G}V_{h}\underset{}{\otimes}W_{h^{-1}g}
;

–

dual: the
g
-graded subspace of
V^{*}
is
(V^{*})_{g}=\left(V_{g^{-1}}\right)^{*}
.

Definition C.5
.

Let
({\cal C},\underset{}{\otimes})
and
({\cal D},\odot)
be unitary fusion categories. A monoidal functor
F:{\cal C}\rightarrow{\cal D}
with monoidal structure
\eta:\odot\circ(F\times F)\Rightarrow F\circ\underset{}{\otimes}
is called unitary if
F
is a
\star
-functor (i.e.,
F
is linear and
F(f^{\dagger})=F(f)^{\dagger}
),
F(\mathbf{1}_{\cal C})
is unitarily isomorphic to
\mathbf{1}_{\cal D}
and
\eta_{X,Y}
is unitary for every
X,Y\in{\cal C}
.

Definition C.6

(Unitary fiber functor)
.

For a tensor category
{\cal C}
, a fiber functor is an exact faithful monoidal functor
{\cal C}\to\mathsf{Vec}
.
For a unitary fusion category
{\cal C}
, we focus on unitary fiber functor which is a unitary monoidal functor
F:{\cal C}\rightarrow\mathsf{Hilb}
(note that the exactness and faithfulness are automatic for a linear functor from a semisimple category).

We now expand the definition of the fiber functor. A unitary fiber functor is a unitary monoidal functor
F:{\cal C}\rightarrow\mathsf{Hilb}
, with

•

a map from objects of
{\cal C}
to objects of
\mathsf{Hilb}
;

•

for each
X,Y
in
{\cal C}
, an injective linear map from
{\cal C}(X,Y)
to
\mathsf{Hilb}(F(X),F(Y))
, ;

•

for each
X,Y
in
{\cal C}
, a unitary natural isomorphism
F_{X,Y}
from
F(X)\underset{}{\otimes}F(Y)
to
F(X\underset{}{\otimes}Y)
,

satisfying the following conditions:

•

for any
X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z
in
{\cal C}
, we have
F(g)F(f)=F(gf)
and
F(\mathrm{id}_{X})=\mathrm{id}_{F(X)}
;

•

F(\mathbf{1})\simeq\mathbb{C}
;

•

for any
X,Y,Z
in
{\cal C}
, the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(X)\underset{}{\otimes}F(Y)\underset{}{\otimes}F(Z)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(X\underset{}{\otimes}Y)\underset{}{\otimes}F(Z)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(X)\underset{}{\otimes}F(Y\underset{}{\otimes}Z)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F((X\underset{}{\otimes}Y)\underset{}{\otimes}Z)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(X\underset{}{\otimes}(Y\underset{}{\otimes}Z))}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{X,Y}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{F(Z)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{F(X)}\underset{}{\otimes}F_{Y,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{X\underset{}{\otimes}Y,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{X,Y\underset{}{\otimes}Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})}

In a word,
a fiber functor is a consistent assignment of Hilbert spaces to objects
. This interpretation is used throughout the paper: each virtual bond of the fusion category MPO assumes a
dual role
—it simultaneously serves as an object in the symmetry category and as a Hilbert space. Similarly, each Hilbert space on a site also plays a
dual role
—it is both an object in the charge category and a Hilbert space.

Definition C.7

(Balanced dual)
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a unitary fusion category and
X\in{\cal C}
,
(X^{*},\mathrm{ev}_{X},\mathrm{coev}_{X})
is called a balanced dual of
X
if

\mathrm{ev}_{X}(\mathrm{id}_{X^{*}}\underset{}{\otimes}f)\mathrm{ev}_{X}^{\dagger}=\mathrm{coev}^{\dagger}_{X}(f\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{X^{*}})\mathrm{coev}_{X}

is satisfied for any
f:X\rightarrow X
.

Theorem C.8

(Tannaka Duality, see
[
59
]
)
.

The assignments

({\cal C},F)\mapsto{\mathsf{H}}={\mathsf{End}}(F),\qquad{\mathsf{H}}\mapsto(\mathsf{Rep}({\mathsf{H}}),\mathrm{fgt})

are mutually inverse bijections between

1.

equivalence classes of finite tensor categories
{\cal C}
with a fiber functor
F
, up to tensor equivalence and isomorphism of tensor functors, and

2.

isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional Hopf algebras.

Algebra

.

(Algebra)
Let
{\cal C}
be a monoidal category. An (associative unital) algebra in
{\cal C}
is a triple
(A,m,\iota)
, consisting of an object
A\in{\cal C}
together with a multiplication
m:A\underset{}{\otimes}A\rightarrow A
and a unit morphism
\iota:\mathbf{1}\rightarrow A
satisfying associativity and identity:

A left
A
-module is defined similarly.

Remark 3
.

Given
A
-modules
M,\,N
in
{\cal C}
, module homomorphisms between them form a subspace
{\cal C}_{A}(M,N)
of the vector space
{\cal C}(M,N)
. The composition of homomorphisms is a homomorphism, thus right
A
-modules in
{\cal C}
form a category
{\cal C}_{A}
.

Definition D.3
.

Given a fusion category
{\cal C}
, and an indecomposible semisimple
{\cal C}
-module
{\cal M}
, denote category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal M})
as
{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\cal M}
and call it the dual fusion category to
{\cal C}
with respect to
{\cal M}
.

Remark 4
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a fusion category. The collection of all
{\cal C}
-module categories forms a 2-category
\mathsf{Mod}({\cal C})
.

Theorem D.4
.

Let
{\cal M}
be a faithful exact module category over a multitensor category
{\cal C}
. The 2-functor

{\cal N}\mapsto\mathsf{Fun}_{\cal C}({\cal M},{\cal N}):\mathsf{Mod}({\cal C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mod}(({\cal C}_{\cal M}^{\vee})^{\text{rev}})

is a 2-equivalence.

Definition D.5

(Categorical Morita equivalence)
.

Let
{\cal C}
,
{\cal D}
be fusion categories.
{\cal C}
and
{\cal D}
are categorically Morita equivalent if there is an indecomposible semisimple
{\cal C}
-module category
{\cal M}
and a monoidal equivalence
{\cal D}^{\text{rev}}\cong{\cal C}^{\vee}_{\cal M}
.

Definition D.6

(Hopf Algebra)
.

Let
{\mathsf{H}}
be a finite-dimensional vector space over
\mathbb{C}
,
m:{\mathsf{H}}\underset{}{\otimes}{\mathsf{H}}\rightarrow{\mathsf{H}}
,
\iota:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow{\mathsf{H}}
,
\Delta:{\mathsf{H}}\rightarrow{\mathsf{H}}\underset{}{\otimes}{\mathsf{H}}
, and
\epsilon:{\mathsf{H}}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
be linear maps, such that
({\mathsf{H}},m,\iota)
is an algebra with multiplication
m
and unit
\iota
and
({\mathsf{H}},\Delta,\epsilon)
is a coalgebra with comultiplication
\Delta
and counit
\epsilon
. If they further satisfy the conditions:

•

\Delta
and
\epsilon
are algebra homomorphisms with the multiplication on
{\mathsf{H}}\underset{}{\otimes}{\mathsf{H}}
be defined as
(m\underset{}{\otimes}m)(\mathrm{id}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{swap}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id})
;

•

Comultiplication of the unit
\mathbf{1}
gives
\mathbf{1}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathbf{1}
;

•

The counit of the unit is
1
:
\epsilon(\mathbf{1})=1
;

the tuple
({\mathsf{H}},m,\iota,\Delta,\epsilon)
is called a bialgebra. If there exists an invertible map (necessarily unique)
S:{\mathsf{H}}\rightarrow{\mathsf{H}}
called the antipode satisfying the condition

S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)}=\epsilon(a)\mathbf{1}=a_{(1)}S(a_{(2)}),

the bialgebra
({\mathsf{H}},m,\iota,\Delta,\epsilon)
is called a Hopf algebra.

Theorem D.7

(See for example, theorem 1.6.6 of
[
91
]
)
.

The following conditions are equivalent for a finite-dimensional unital complex
\star
-algebra
A
:

1.

A
is a C
⋆
-algebra;

2.

There exists a
\star
-homomorphism
A\simeq\oplus_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{M}_{a_{i}}
, where each summand has the usual conjugate transpose
\dagger
-operation;

3.

For every
a\in A
,
aa^{\star}=0
implies
a=0
.

Hopf C
⋆
-algebra is defined in
[
92
]
, and a version of C
⋆
-quantum groupoid is defined in
[
61
]
.

Appendix E
Operator algebraic description of ground state

Example 7
.

Consider the 1D quantum Ising model in symmetry breaking phase, characterized by the local interaction:

H_{\Lambda}=\sum_{\{i,i+1\}\subset\Lambda}\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{1}-Z_{i}Z_{i+1}\right)

for any finite region
\Lambda\in\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{f}
. Let
p_{i,i+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{1}-Z_{i}Z_{i+1}\right)
. It can be verified that the
H
-type ground state
\omega
satisfying
\omega(p_{i,i+1})=0
is an
O
-type ground state
[
68
]
and the space of
H
-type ground states forms a simplex
[0,1]
whose extreme points
0
and
1
are two superselection sectors, corresponding to
\langle\cdots 00000\cdots|(-)|\cdots 00000\cdots\rangle
and
\langle\cdots 11111\cdots|(-)|\cdots 11111\cdots\rangle
, respectively.
What might be counterintuitive is that the single domain wall state, with the domain wall located at the link
(0,1)
, defined by

\omega=\langle\cdots 00001111\cdots|(-)|\cdots 00001111\cdots\rangle

is also a ground state in
V.1
. We now verify it.

For an arbitrary
O\in\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda}
, if
\Lambda\subset\mathbb{Z}_{>1}
(or
\Lambda\subset\mathbb{Z}_{<0}
), the ground state condition is given by

\omega(O^{\dagger}H_{\overline{\Lambda}}O)-0\geq 0.

which is trivially satisfied by the positivity of
H_{\overline{\Lambda}}
. When
\overline{\Lambda}
crosses the regions
\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}
and
\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the ground state condition becomes

\omega\left(O^{\dagger}[H_{\overline{\Lambda}},O]\right)=\omega\left(O^{\dagger}H_{\overline{\Lambda}}O\right)-\omega\left(O^{\dagger}O\right)\geq 0.

If
\omega\left(O^{\dagger}O\right)=0
, the inequality is satisfied by the positivity of
H_{\overline{\Lambda}}
. If
\omega\left(O^{\dagger}O\right)>0
, define

|\eta\rangle:=O\bigg|0[00\cdots 0011\cdots 11]1\bigg\rangle\in(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes|\overline{\Lambda}|},

above condition is then equivalent to

\frac{\langle\eta|H_{\overline{\Lambda}}|\eta\rangle}{\langle\eta|\eta\rangle}\geq 1.

We use the square bracket to denote the region
\Lambda
.
This inequality is satisfied because operators supported on
\Lambda
can not annihilate a single domain wall; they can only move or create a pair of the domain walls within
\overline{\Lambda}
, thus the energy of
|\eta\rangle
can only be larger or equal to the energy of
\bigg|0[0\cdots 01\cdots 1]1\bigg\rangle
. This ground state property is fundamentally linked to the topological nature of the single domain wall state.

Appendix F
Q-system

Following
[
93
]
, the Q-system is defined as follows:

Definition F.1

(Q-system)
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a unitary fusion category. A Q-system in
{\cal C}
is a triple
(A,m,\iota)
, where

1.

(A,m,\iota)
is a unital associative isometric algebra in
{\cal C}
and;

2.

m
and
m^{\dagger}
satisfy the Frobenius condition;

3.

\mathrm{ev}_{A}:=\iota^{\dagger}m:A\underset{}{\otimes}A\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
and
\mathrm{coev}_{A}:=m^{\dagger}\iota:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow A\underset{}{\otimes}A
is the balanced dual (see
C.7
) for
A
.

It has been proved in
[
94
,
95
,
96
,
45
]
that 1
\Rightarrow
2.
And condition 3 implies that
A
is symmetrically self-dual, see for example
[
97
,
93
]
. We denote
m_{(n)}
by multiplying
n
copies of
A
’s to a single
A
.

Definition F.2

(Irreducible Q-system, see for example Lemma 3.13 of
[
96
]
)
.

A Q-system
(A,m,\iota)
in a unitary fusion category
{\cal C}
is called irreducible if
\dim{\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A)=1
.

Motivated by Lemma 3.16 of
[
96
]
, we define

Definition F.3
.

Let
(A,m,\iota)
be a simple Q-system in a unitary fusion category
{\cal C}
, then the tuple
({\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A),\cdot,\iota,\star)
is a finite-dimensional unital associative
\star
-algebra with

•

multiplication:
f\cdot g:=m(f\underset{}{\otimes}g)
for any
f,g\in{\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A)
;

•

unit:
\iota\cdot f=f\cdot\iota=f
for any
f
;

•

star:
f^{\star}:=(f^{\dagger}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})m^{\dagger}\iota=(\mathrm{id}_{A}\underset{}{\otimes}f^{\dagger})m^{\dagger}\iota
for any
f
.

It is a C
⋆
-algebra by the theorem
D.7

f\cdot f^{\star}=0\Rightarrow\iota^{\dagger}m(f\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})(\iota^{\dagger}m(f\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A}))^{\dagger}=0\Rightarrow\iota^{\dagger}m(f\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})=0\Rightarrow f=0.

By Lemma 3.17 of
[
96
]
:

Proposition F.4
.

There is a
\star
-isomorphism

\displaystyle{\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A)\simeq{\cal C}_{\mathbf{1}|A}(A,A)

\displaystyle f\mapsto m(f\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})

\displaystyle g\circ\iota\mapsfrom g.

Similarly, there is also a
*
-isomorphism
{\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A)\simeq{\cal C}_{A|\mathbf{1}}(A,A)
.

Definition F.5

(Modules)
.

Let
{\cal C}
be a unitary fusion category and
(A,m,\iota)
a Q-system in
{\cal C}
. The left (right)
A
-module
(M,m_{M})
(
(N,{}_{N}m)
) is called a Q-system module if
m_{M}
(
{}_{N}m
) is partial isometric.

By the Definition 3.37 of
[
96
]

We now review the Morita equivalence between Q-systems.

Definition F.7

(Morita equivalence)
.

Let
A,B
be Q-systems in
{\cal C}
. Then
A
and
B
are called Morita equivalent if there is an
A
-
B
-bimodule
M
and a
B
-
A
-bimodule
N
such that
M\underset{B}{\otimes}N\simeq A
and
N\underset{A}{\otimes}M\simeq B
.

Remark 5

(
[
98
]
)
.

Suppose
A
and
B
are Morita equivalent by an
A
-
B
-bimodule
M
and a
B
-
A
-bimodule
N
, then one can construct a larger Q-system

X=\begin{pmatrix}A&M\\
N&B\end{pmatrix}:=A\oplus M\oplus N\oplus B,

whose algebra structure is the multiplication by block.

We review the definition of the simple Q-system.

Definition F.8

(Simple Q-system)
.

The Q-system
(A,m,\iota)
in
{\cal C}
is called simple if
A

{\cal C}_{A|A}
.

Proposition F.11
.

Let
(A,m,\iota)
be a simple Q-system and
p
a projector in
({\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A),\cdot,\iota,\star)
. Suppose
m(p\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})
splits as
r^{\dagger}r
with
r:A\rightarrow A_{r}
,
m(\mathrm{id}_{A}\underset{}{\otimes}p)
splits as
l^{\dagger}l
with
l:A\rightarrow A_{l}
, and
m_{(2)}(p\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A}\underset{}{\otimes}p)
splits as
P^{\dagger}P
with
P:A\rightarrow A_{P}
. Then

•

(A_{P},m_{P},\iota_{P})
is a Q-system in
{\cal C}
, where

m_{P}:=Pm(P^{\dagger}\underset{}{\otimes}P^{\dagger})\times\sqrt{\frac{d_{A}}{|p^{\dagger}p|}},\quad\iota_{P}:=P\iota\times\sqrt{\frac{|p^{\dagger}p|}{d_{A}}}.

•

(A_{l},\mu,\mu_{l})
is an
A
-
A_{P}
-bimodule,
(A_{r},\nu_{r},\nu)
is an
A_{P}
-
A
-bimodule, where

\mu:=lm(\mathrm{id}_{A}\underset{}{\otimes}l^{\dagger}),\quad\mu_{r}:=lm(l^{\dagger}\underset{}{\otimes}P^{\dagger})\times\sqrt{\frac{d_{A}}{|p^{\dagger}p|}},\quad\nu_{r}:=rm(P^{\dagger}\underset{}{\otimes}r^{\dagger})\times\sqrt{\frac{d_{A}}{|p^{\dagger}p|}},\quad\nu:=rm(r^{\dagger}\underset{}{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A}).

•

A
and
A_{P}
are Morita equivalent by
A_{r}
and
A_{l}
.

Such a circular commutativity does not hold for any local operators but only for those that are in the fixed point already.
Moreover, given any
f\in\mathfrak{Z}(A)
, its Hermitian conjugate
f^{\dagger}
is also in
\mathfrak{Z}(A)
. Thus
\mathfrak{Z}(A)
is a finite-dimensional commutative C
⋆
-algebra.

Since any finite-dimensional commutative C
⋆
-algebra is isomorphic to direct sums of
\mathbb{C}
, we decompose the algebra to
\mathfrak{Z}(A)\simeq\oplus_{\alpha}\mathbb{C}p_{\alpha}
, with the set
\{p_{\alpha}\}
be the set of orthogonal projectors satisfying
p_{\alpha}p_{\beta}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}p_{\alpha}
and
p_{\alpha}^{\dagger}=p_{\alpha}
. These projectors satisfy the property that they can freely proliferate on any
A
-mesh:

Corollary G.2
.

The
H
-type ground state space
\mathcal{G}_{\mathbb{Z}}
of the Q-system model
(\mathbb{Z},A,1-m^{\dagger}m)
is a simplex, whose extreme points are
\omega_{\alpha}
, satisfying
\omega_{\alpha}(m_{i,i+1}^{\dagger}m_{i,i+1})=1
for any
i
and
\omega_{\alpha}\left(p_{\beta}\right)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}
for
p_{\beta}
on any site.

Proof.

Denote
p_{\alpha,\{0\}}
the projector on site
0
, let
\lambda_{\alpha}=\omega(p_{\alpha,\{0\}})\geq 0
, for any finite support operator
O\in\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda}
and
\omega
a ground state,

\displaystyle\omega(O)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}\omega(p_{\alpha,\{0\}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}c_{\alpha}\lambda_{\beta}\omega_{\beta}(p_{\alpha,\{0\}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\beta}\lambda_{\beta}\omega_{\beta}(O).

Thus any ground state
\omega
can be expressed as a finite convex combination of
\omega_{\alpha}
:

\omega=\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}\omega_{\alpha},\quad\lambda_{\alpha}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}=1.

∎

Similar to the
G
-SPT case, the ground state of the
({\cal C},f)
-symmetric phase can also be represented by a matrix product state (MPS)
[
37
]
.
Suppose
(A,m,\iota)
is a Q-system in
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
and

G.2
Generic edge modes

Suppose
(A,m_{A},\iota_{A}),(B,m_{B},\iota_{B})

\mathsf{Hilb}
and
(M,\mu_{A},\mu_{B})
a
A
-
B
bimodule. Let

\Psi(\{i\})=\begin{cases}A&i<0\\
M&i=0\\
B&i>0\end{cases}

and

\Phi(\{i,i+1\})=\begin{cases}1-m_{A}^{\dagger}m_{A}&i<-1\\
1-\mu_{A}^{\dagger}\mu_{A}&i=-1\\
1-\mu_{B}^{\dagger}\mu_{B}&i=0\\
1-m_{B}^{\dagger}m_{B}&i>0\end{cases}.

The triple
(\mathbb{Z},\Psi,\Phi)
defines a 1D quantum system on an infinite chain describing the domain wall
M
between the phase
A

The map
\mathrm{scr}
is an idempotent and its image
\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{scr})=:\mathfrak{Z}_{A|B}(M)
is called the algebra of fixed-point operators on the domain wall. By the property of the Q-system model, we have

\omega=\omega\circ\mathrm{scr}.

Thus the
H
-type ground state space is isomorphic to the space of states on
\mathfrak{Z}_{A|B}(M)=\mathrm{End}_{A|B}(M)
. And
\mathfrak{Z}(A)=\mathfrak{Z}_{A|A}(A)
,
\mathfrak{Z}_{A}(M)=\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{1}|A}(M)
as special cases. We thus have:

The zero mode of
(\mathbb{Z},\Psi,\Phi)
is the minimal faithful module over the algebra of fixed-point operators on the domain wall
\mathfrak{Z}_{A|B}(M)
.

G.3
Ground state degeneracy by taking the thermodynamic limit

We now calculate the ground state degeneracy of the Q-system model by taking the thermodynamic limit.

Let
\{{\cal L}_{L}\}_{L=4}^{\infty}
be a sequence of quantum systems, where each
{\cal L}_{L}:=(\{1,\cdots,L\},\Psi,\Phi)
represents a quantum system defined on the lattice
\{1,\cdots,L\}
. This sequence corresponds to the process of taking the thermodynamic limit.
In general, both the bulk and the edge contribute to the ground state degeneracy of each finite chain
{\cal L}_{L}
. Our goal is to distinguish these contributions.

Both the bulk and the edge include regions containing a macroscopic number of sites, growing proportionally with the system size as the system itself grows. This perspective is what we refer to as “macroscopically local”, and we provide a more detailed characterization below.

A macroscopic local region in one dimension is a sequence of local regions
\{\Lambda_{L}\}_{L=4}^{\infty}
, where
\Lambda_{L}\subset\{1,\cdots,L\}
such that the following limits exist

\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\min(\Lambda_{L})/L:=d_{l},\quad\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}|\Lambda_{L}|/L:=|\Lambda|>0.

We also define

d_{r}:=1-d_{l}-|\Lambda|.

The
d_{l}
(
d_{r}
) characterizes the left (right) distance between the left (right) boundary of the region and that of the system and
|\Lambda|
characterizes the length of the region.
The macroscopic local region
\{\Lambda_{L}\}_{L=4}^{\infty}
is

•

a bulk region if
0<d_{l}<1
and
0<d_{r}<1
;

•

a left boundary region if
\min(\Lambda_{L})=0
for any
L
and
0<d_{r}<1
;

•

a right boundary region if
\max(\Lambda_{L})=L-1
for any
L
and
0<d_{l}<1
.

Figure 5:
Illustration of the macroscopic local regions. Here the green region represents the left boundary, the blue region represents the bulk and the grey region represents the right boundary.

To calculate the bulk and boundary ground state degeneracies separately, we adopt the principle that
the ground state degeneracy in a macroscopically local region is the effective degeneracy observed by its local observables
. This principle is inspired by the philosophical exploration of the principle that
a phase is defined on an open disk
presented in
[
100
]
and the entanglement bootstrap framework discussed in
[
101
,
102
]
.

The observable within a macroscopic local region is a sequence of C
⋆
-algebras
\{\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}\}_{L=4}^{\infty}
7
7

7

An ideal formulation of the thermodynamic limit requires specifying embedding maps between the C
⋆
-algebras for different
L
values, so that models with varying numbers of sites can be meaningfully compared. The total algebra in the thermodynamic limit is then the inductive limit of this inductive net.

, with the natural embedding of algebras
\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}\hookrightarrow\mathfrak{A}_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}
for each
L
. Any states on
\mathfrak{A}_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}
can be restricted to
\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}
. In particular, the restriction of the global ground states

8
8

8

Note that for a non-fixed-point model, the ground state is generically not exactly degenerate. Still, for a fixed
L
there exist energy gaps
E_{i,L}
between the ground state and several excitation states labeled by
i
, such that
\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}E_{i,L}=0
for all
i
. In this case, an error is needed to include the energy states that are sufficiently low as the ground state subspace when taking the thermodynamic limit
[
108
]
. We will not deal with this case here.

defines an effective space of ground states on local regions
[
105
]

\displaystyle{\cal G}_{\Lambda_{L}}:=\left\{\omega|_{\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}}:\omega\in{\cal G}_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}\right\}.

This restriction may not be injective; there may exist two distinct ground states
\omega\neq\omega^{\prime}
on
\mathfrak{A}_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}
that become identical on
\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}
after restriction:

\omega|_{\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}}=\omega^{\prime}|_{\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}}.

If the geometric property of the space
{\cal G}_{\Lambda_{L}}
stabilizes as
L\to+\infty
, then the ground state degeneracy and the associated superselection sectors can be inferred from this stabilized geometry.

The argument above may be too vague. Now we consider the Q-system model as a specific example. Since it is a fixed-point model, this case is clean and almost trivial.
Let
(A,m,\iota)
be a Q-system in
{\cal C}_{\mathsf{Hilb}_{f}}^{\vee}
and
(M,m_{M})
,
(N,{}_{N}m)
are standard
A
-modules. Consider a sequence
\left\{\mathcal{L}_{L}\right\}_{L=4}^{\infty}
, where
{\cal L}_{L}=(\{1,2,\cdots,L\},\Psi_{L},\Phi_{L})
is the Q-system model on a finite chain
with left boundary condition
M
, right boundary condition
N
and the bulk
A
.
We know that the ground state subspace of
{\cal L}_{L}
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{fgt}(M\underset{A}{\otimes}N)
for all
L
.

We denote the map

m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}:=\bigg(M\underset{}{\otimes}A^{\otimes(L-2)}\underset{}{\otimes}N\rightarrow M\underset{}{\otimes}A\underset{}{\otimes}N\rightrightarrows\\
M\underset{}{\otimes}N\rightarrow M\underset{A}{\otimes}N\bigg).

Given a fixed
L
, ground states of
{\cal L}_{L}
are equivalent to density matrices over
M\underset{A}{\otimes}N
.
Suppose
\rho\in\mathrm{End}(M\underset{A}{\otimes}N)
is a density matrix, the map

\rho\mapsto m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}^{\dagger}\rho m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}

carries a density matrix on
M\underset{A}{\otimes}N
to a density matrix on
M\underset{}{\otimes}A^{\otimes(L-2)}\underset{}{\otimes}N
. And the ground state valued on
O\in\mathfrak{A}_{\Lambda_{L}}
is

\omega(O)=\mathrm{Tr}\bigg(m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}^{\dagger}\rho m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}O\bigg)\\
=\mathrm{Tr}\bigg(\rho m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}Om_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}^{\dagger}\bigg).

•

When
\{\Lambda_{L}\}
is a bulk region, there exists a number
x>0
and
N\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
\min(\Lambda_{L})>Lx
, and
\max(\Lambda_{L})<L(1-x)
for all
L>N
. Thus for sufficiently large
L
, the region
\Lambda_{L}
will be surrounded by
A
’s. Thus

\omega(O)=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}Om_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}^{\dagger})\\
=\mathrm{Tr}\left(\rho m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}\mathrm{scr}(O)m_{\{1,\cdots,L\}}^{\dagger}\right)

Suppose
\mathrm{scr}(O)=\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}
is the decomposition of bimodule maps, the equation above can be reduced to

\omega(O)=\omega\left(\mathrm{scr}(O)\right)=\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}\omega(p_{\alpha}),\quad\forall L>N.

Thus the value of
\omega
on local operators in
\Lambda_{L}
is completely fixed by
\omega(p_{\alpha})
, implying the state space
{\cal G}_{\Lambda_{L}}
is a simplex for all
L>N
. We thus conclude that the ground state space on the macroscopic local region is a simplex, whose dimension is
\dim(\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A))-1
. Thus the dimension of
\mathfrak{Z}(\mathrm{fgt}A)
is the ground state subspace in the bulk, and whose extreme points are superselection sectors;

•

When
\{\Lambda_{L}\}
is a left boundary region, there exists a number
x>0
and
N\in N
, such that
\max(\Lambda_{L})<L(1-x)
for all
L>N
. Thus for sufficiently large
L
, the region
\Lambda_{L}
will be surrounded by
A
’s on the right-hand side. By the Equation (
V.3
)

\omega(O)=\omega\left(\mathrm{scr}(O)\right),\quad\forall L>N.

Since
\mathrm{scr}(O)\in\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
, the value of
\omega
on local operators on
\Lambda_{L}
is totally given by its value on operators in
\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
. Thus, the edge mode is the minimal faithful module over
\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{fgt}A}(\mathrm{fgt}M)
.

•

The right boundary region case is the same.

These results are consistent with the infinite chain calculations in the last section.

G.4

(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A,-m^{\dagger}m)

(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A_{P},-m_{P}^{\dagger}m_{P})
constructed from the reduced Q-system
(A_{P},m_{P},\iota_{P})
without causing phase transition.

\lambda_{A}=d_{A}^{-1}|f^{\dagger}f|\geq 0
and
\lambda_{f}=0
if and only if
f=0
.

The quantum system

{\cal L}_{f}:=\left(\mathbb{Z},{\mathsf{H}},A,-m(f)^{\dagger}m(f)\right)

is a gapped commuting model for each
f\in{\cal C}(\mathbf{1},A)\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}
. By

(-m(f)^{\dagger}m(f))^{2}=\frac{|f^{\dagger}f|}{d_{A}}m(f)^{\dagger}m(f),

the energy gap is
\frac{|f^{\dagger}f|}{d_{A}}>0
.
Thus a continuous class of the non-isolated fixed-point models can be realized whenever
A
is simple and reducible. The phenomenon of the non-isolated fixed-point first appeared in
[
106
]
by the corner-double-line tensor and further been seriously treated in
[
1
]
by the so-called
entanglement filtering
procedure. Our local interaction here can be viewed as a type of the corner-double-line tensor in Hamiltonian mechanics and
f
is the the tensor in the corner.
